Hi Stan-users. See below. If this project interests anybody, feel free to contact Allan Debertin directly.
A

>> On Jan 28, 2015, at 11:11 AM, Allan Debertin <adeb...@uoguelph.ca> wrote:
>>
>> Dear Dr. Andrew Gelman,
>>
>> I am a PhD candidate at the University of Guelph, in Guelph, Canada and my thesis investigates mechanisms that could explain why the Ontario Lake Erie Gillnet Fishery persists to harvest top-trophic level fishes, whereas in other systems top-trophic level fisheries have collapsed. One of my thesis chapters gathers fishery stock assessments for two different species White Perch (non-native to Lake Erie) and White Bass to estimate the total abundance of these species through a time series.
>>
>> The theme of the stock assessment chapter is to examine the trade-offs between model complexity towards parameter estimation and parsimony of model information. Model complexity affects reliability in two important ways. Use of low-parameter models may mask underlying dynamics such that harvest policies deemed to be conservative actually lead to greater risk, or vice versa. However, decision-making based on over-parameterized models may similarly put stocks at risk, leading to pleas for model parsimony. To evaluate reliability, three stock assessment models will be ranked in retrospective analyses using information theoretic approaches. We expect to see with increasing model complexity we would have have better parameter estimates (e.g. smaller credible intervals), however, we expect an inverse relationship with parsimony (i.e. as models become more complex, we would expect greater Information Criterion scores).
>>
>> I was going to use JAGS to run three state-space stock assessment models, i) surplus production model (least complex), ii) age-structured sequential population model, iii) an integrated, age-structured, length-based model (most complex) to gather parameter estimates and rank these model using Deviance Information Criterion (DIC). However, the DIC scores for the most complex models are negative (suggests a poor model fit), and I've read a few articles that WAIC may be more useful information criterion when comparing non-nested models.
>>
>> I have developed code in STAN to calculate WAIC for the first two models i) surplus-production model and ii) age-structured sequential population models, but I am having difficulty properly coding the third iii) integrated model. I'm not even sure if it can be coded in STAN due to looping structures that require sequential order of command lines in STAN. I have been reading and have posted a few articles on the STAN google forum, and noticed that you are now a proponent of STAN, and in particular the use and development of easier to use WAIC calculations. I'm wondering, if you would be interested in helping me with developing the proper coding in STAN for the last integrated-stock assessment model to determine the WAIC. If so, I would offer co-authorship on any potential peer-reviewed journal articles.
>>
>> Let me know if you are interested in this collaboration and I can send the code I have been working on for all three models. We should also a schedule a online meeting to go through the troubleshooting of the code, since I would like to understand STAN a little better.
>>
>> Best regards,
>>
>> Allan Debertin
>> --
>> Allan Debertin, MSc
>> PhD Candidate
>> Integrative Biology
>> University of Guelph
>

Hi Bob,

 I'll post that code ASAP, I have the last (most complex) model mostly complied where the STAN code successfully compiles in C++.

In the meantime, I was wondering if you or others could look at whether I correctly coded calculating WAIC for the first, least complex model, the  surplus production model (I showed this model in an earlier post). For a joint distribution of the parameters I'm pretty certain I multiply the likelihoods for each part of the State-Space model.

Many Thanks,

Allan

See below for code:


### WAIC functions
colVars <- function(a) {n <-  dim(a)[[1]]; 
                        c <- dim(a)[[2]]; 
                        return(.colMeans(((a - matrix(.colMeans(a, n, c), nrow = n, 
                                                      ncol = c, byrow = TRUE)) ^ 2), n, c) * n / (n - 1))}



waic <- function(stanfit){
  log_lik <- extract (stanfit, "log_lik")$log_lik
  dim(log_lik) <- if (length(dim(log_lik))==1) c(length(log_lik),1) else
    c(dim(log_lik)[1], prod(dim(log_lik)[2:length(dim(log_lik))]))
  S <- nrow(log_lik)
  n <- ncol(log_lik)
  lpd <- log(colMeans(exp(log_lik)))
  p_waic <- colVars(log_lik)
  elpd_waic <- lpd - p_waic
  waic <- -2*elpd_waic
  loo_weights_raw <- 1/exp(log_lik-max(log_lik))
  loo_weights_normalized <- loo_weights_raw/
    matrix(colMeans(loo_weights_raw),nrow=S,ncol=n,byrow=TRUE)
  loo_weights_regularized <- pmin (loo_weights_normalized, sqrt(S))
  elpd_loo <- log(colMeans(exp(log_lik)*loo_weights_regularized)/
                    colMeans(loo_weights_regularized))
  p_loo <- lpd - elpd_loo
  pointwise <- cbind(waic,lpd,p_waic,elpd_waic,p_loo,elpd_loo)
  total <- colSums(pointwise)
  se <- sqrt(n*colVars(pointwise))
  return(list(waic=total["waic"], elpd_waic=total["elpd_waic"],
              p_waic=total["p_waic"], elpd_loo=total["elpd_loo"], p_loo=total["p_loo"],
              pointwise=pointwise, total=total, se=se))
}



#########

library(rstan)

sink("surplus.stan")
cat("
data {
  int<lower=0> N; 
  real L[N];
  real I1[N];
  real I2[N];
}
parameters {
  real<lower=0.001> k;
  real<lower=0> r;
  real<lower=0> P[N];
  real<lower=0, upper=1> sigma2p;
  real<lower=0, upper=1> tau2s1;
  real<lower=0, upper=1> tau2s2;
  real<lower=0.0001> iq1;
  real<lower=0.0001> iq2;
}
transformed parameters {
  real<lower=0> q1;
  real<lower=0> Q1;
  real<lower=0> q2;
  real<lower=0> Q2;
  real<lower=0> K;
  K <- 1/k;
  q1 <- 1/iq1;
  Q1 <- q1*K;
  q2 <- 1/iq2;
  Q2 <- q2*K;
}
model {
  k ~ lognormal(-3.342306,0.2704328);
  r ~ uniform(0.0001,3);
  iq1 ~ gamma(0.001,0.001);
  iq2 ~ gamma(0.001,0.001);
  sigma2p ~ inv_gamma(14.038902,8.4565988);
  tau2s1 ~ inv_gamma(3.7730903,0.47829205);
  tau2s2 ~ inv_gamma(3.7730903,0.28697523);

// state equation
// **************
  {
  real Pmu[N];
  Pmu[1] <- 0;
  P[1] ~ lognormal(Pmu[1], pow(sigma2p, -0.5));
    for (i in 2:N) {
      Pmu[i] <- log(fmax(P[i-1] + r*P[i-1]*(1-P[i-1]) - k*L[i-1], 0.01));
      P[i] ~ lognormal(Pmu[i], pow(sigma2p, -0.5));
    }
  } 

// observation equation
// ********************
    for (i in 1:N) {
      real mu[N];
      mu[i] <- log(Q1*P[i]);
      I1[i] ~ lognormal(mu[i], pow(tau2s1,-0.5));      
    }
    for (i in 9:N) {
      real mu[N];
      mu[i] <- log(Q2*P[i]);
      I2[i] ~ lognormal(mu[i], pow(tau2s2, -0.5));
    }
}
generated quantities {
  real B[N];
  real MSP;
  vector [N] log_lik1;
  vector [N] log_lik2;    
  vector [N] log_lik3;
  vector [N] log_lik;
    for (i in 1:N){
      B[i] <- K*P[i];
    }
    MSP <- r*K/4;

//Log_likelihoods of State and observation models
    for (n in 1:N){
      log_lik1[n] <- lognormal_log(I1[n], log(Q1*P[n]), pow(tau2s1, -0.5));
    }
    for (n in 9:N){
      log_lik2[n] <- lognormal_log(I2[n], log(Q2*P[n]), pow(tau2s2, -0.5));
    }
  {
  log_lik3[1] <- lognormal_log(P[1], 0, pow(sigma2p,-0.5));
      for (n in 2:N){
        log_lik3[n] <- lognormal_log(P[n],log(fmax(P[n-1] + r*P[n-1]*(1-P[n-1]) - k*L[n-1], 0.01)), pow(sigma2p, -0.5));
      }
  }
    for (n in 1:N){
      log_lik[n] <-  (log_lik1[n]*log_lik2[n]*log_lik3[n]);
    }
}
    ", fill=TRUE) 
sink()

            model_name = 'whiteperch')

                      L=c(3.10,  3.62,  2.80,  1.07,  1.57, 0.80, 0.54, 0.35, 0.56,

                             0.073, 0.074,0.096,0.165, 0.185, 0.172, 0.123, 0.099, 0.108, 0.143, 0.160, 0.190),
                      I2=c(-1, -1, -1, -1, -1, -1, -1, -1, 9.66,  4.23, 7.36, 19.51, 41.17,
                           36.18, 40.21, 49.86, 43.76, 88.38, 78.27, 67.00, 75.78, 47.36, 69.47, 32.11))

One thing you can't do in these models is declare a parameter
more loosely than its support in the model.

> real<lower=0> r;

> r ~ uniform(0.0001,3);

This can cause problems at the lower and higher ends in Stan.
With that uniform distribution, the declaration should be:

real<lower=0.0001,upper=3> r;

At which point the uniform's redundant, because that's the default.

But we don't recommend these bounded priors or the diffuse
gamma priors you're using --- see the manual chapter on regression,
which has several sections on the priors we do recommend with
some discussion.

And if you were trying to provide conjugate priors, they shouldn't
be inverse gamma on precision, but gamma. But Stan doesn't do
anything special with conjugate priors, so they're not necessary or
even beneficial for speed.

inv(x) is a bit more efficient than 1/x.

You shouldn't do the same calculation in loops:

> for (n in 1:N){
> log_lik1[n] <- lognormal_log(I1[n], log(Q1*P[n]), pow(tau2s1, -0.5));
> }

This should be:

{
real inv_sqrt_tau2s1;
inv_sqrt_tau2s1 <- inv_sqrt(ta2s1);
for (n in 1:N)

log_lik1[n] <- lognormal_log(I1[n], log(Q1 * P[n]), inv_sqrt_tau2s1);
}

Stan can reuse the computation and it saves both time and space.

Using fmax() in a Stan model is *VERY DANGEROUS*. You should
be enforcing the constraint with a constraint directly. Doing
what you're doing with fmax will mess up gradient calculations
when it returns a constant. It also doesn't make sense in the model.

I'm afraid I don't know much about WAIC. So no help with your
direct question.

I would highly recommend starting from a simpler model and building
up this more complex one.

- Bob

Hi Bob,

I finished coding the most complex integrated stock assessment model in STAN and got it to successfully compile in C++. However, I'm getting error messages with the Dirichlet functions as the sum of probabilities need to add to 1. This might be a fundamental difference with the JAGS/BUS Dirichlet function and the STAN code, or the code I'm using from JAGS isn't appropriate.   Anyway, below I post the JAGS code, STAN code, and a sample of the error message.

Here is the JAGS code for the Integrated model (modified from Mäntyniemi et al. 2013 Can. J. Fish. Aquat. Sci. 70: 1317–1326)

model{

#######################################################
# Population dynamics
# The population dynamics model tracks the total number
# in the population through time. The time step is one year (y)
#

The argument to the Dirichlet is a simplex, so if

theta ~ dirichlet(alpha);

then theta needs to sum to 1. If it's a parameter, declare
it as a simplex. If not, it needs to be normalized somehow.
softmax() will map a general set of linear predictors to a
simplex.

I'd strongly suggest starting by getting simple models working
then building up to more complex models. It's harder to debug
something complex.

- Bob

Our matrix division is the usual one:

A/B = A * inverse(B)

JAGS followed R in straying from usual notation and I

You'll have to write that code by hand. Stan doesn't
automatically broadcast like R does. The reason is that
it's a very dangerous coding practice because of the way it
hides potential errors.

Here's a function that should work (I haven't tried to
compile or test it):

matrix row_div(matrix a, vector b) {
matrix[rows(a), cols(a)] result;
for (m in 1:rows(a))
result[m] <- a[m] / b[m];
return result;
}

Or you could just write the same thing inline in the code
where you need it.

Of course, requiring users to write loop-based code is also
error prone, but we decided that was the better course than
potentially hiding errors. What we really need is a unit-testing
framework for Stan functions so that users could debug them before
dropping them into models.
